utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your evidence will now continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration to tell the truth which you made at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Now Mr. Scully will continue with his examination. Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dashi.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: On Monday we were discussing a KLA unit in Stagovo village. Did you personally ever assist that unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said earlier that this was something that we spontaneously -- that was spontaneously created, and I didn't know what was going on elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Directing your attention to the unit that spontaneously formed within the village, did you have any role with that unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. I had this observation point. We only observed from that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Who was observing from the observation point?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the observation point there were four shifts, myself and Muhamet and Shabedin did one shift of four hours, but there were other people who came and did other shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And those people who were at the observation point, were they different from the people who were in the KLA unit?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were all civilians. We did not have guns. I told you earlier we had only one M-48, but we never used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And did you have uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not. Not only myself but the others as well in the observation point. Nobody had uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And you said you had an M-48 rifle. Did that weapon work?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not know because we never tried it, but we saw that later, that the barrel was not in order, in working order. So after the offensive it -- we saw that it would not have worked. That rifle was never used. It wouldn't function even if it were used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: On what date did you and these other civilians start your work at the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the date, but it was about 10 to 12 days before the offensive of the 21st of March -- of May.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And where in relation to the village of Stagovo was this post located?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the outskirts of Stagova. There are places that are called Fushet e Stagov [phoen], the Stagov fields, where the Serbian army was stationed. We feared that the forces would come from the main road and enter Stagova, and that's what we observed mostly. At the same time there was an influx of other citizens coming from the surrounding areas so we could observe them as well coming from the other villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Could you see both the main road and the village from the observation post?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the village, but the road. From the main road there are two roads that come into the village. One is called Rruga e Kuqe and the other one that goes to the martyrs' cemetery. Both of them we could see very well. This is -- I meant the main road from Ferizaj to Kacanik and then Skup [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Other than the two roads you could see from the observation post, is there any other means of getting into the village of Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no other road. There is a foot-path that links Biceci and Stagova and other villages, but this was only a foot-path. But there is no other road where you can use a vehicle on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Were you in that observation post on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Who was there with you at about 4.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At 4.00 in the morning, together with me were Shabedin Dashi and Muhamet Dashi. I almost forgot his name now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did anything happen at about 4.00 in the morning on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't keep a watch, so maybe I will not be very accurate in the times, but at about 4.00 we could hear the vehicles coming from the main road. And then this noise came to this Stagova road and then the forces got off the vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: About how many vehicles did you hear coming up the road?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could not see the vehicles because it's uphill and they did not come to the flat part, but they stopped somewhere and the forces got off. I don't know how many vehicles there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Was it more than one?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't want to make a mistake here. But there were many because -- more than one because there were many people, many forces. So it couldn't be only one vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Where did the forces go after they got out of the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The observation point was at Mahalla e Gudaqeve, and I went to get a glass of water or light a cigarette - I don't remember what I did - but I saw them when they were there at the Mahalla e Gudaqeve and also in the mountain nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: About how many people did you see at Mahalla e Gudaqeve?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you the number, but there were many.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And could you see what they were wearing at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were policemen. They were wearing police uniforms. But then around them outside the village the army was stationed there, they were guarding there. But the action in the village was carried out by the police. Their uniforms were dark blue or dark green. I'm not very good with colours, I'm sorry. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the uniform the police normally wore in your municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar. I did not pay too much attention to those uniforms, but I -- as I say, I did not pay attention to colours. What I saw was that on the arm it wrote "milicija," and I told you the approximate colours they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Were the uniforms the people you've described as police wearing the same ones the police in your municipality normally wore?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Earlier, when there was some kind of state of emergency, they had those camouflage uniforms; while in peacetimes, in normal times, they had the same uniform, it did not change, the regular police uniform. Only in state of emergency they had this camouflage uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: The uniform that the people were -- the police were wearing on the 21st was the uniform you'd seen in a state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is leading.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree. Well, it's a pretty useless answer now. This is pretty hopeless evidence at the moment, I have to say, Mr. Scully. It's not very instructive, but do your best.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: You stated that the army was stationed around the village. How long had the army been stationed there?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The army was in the fields of Stagova; it was positioned there. The tanks were lined up. I did not see any artillery, but the tanks I saw there. And when NATO attacked, whether they were eliminated or bombed or whether they left, I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Do you know if the army -- do you know the location of the army on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around the main road. According to eye-witnesses, on the 21st of May, the day of the offensive, we were explained this later --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. You've been asked what you saw from an observation post around 4.00 in the morning of the 21st of May. Could you concentrate on that, please, and tell us what you actually saw yourself happening at that time. Then we'll move on to other things. But I'm finding it very difficult to follow any of what you're saying so far. So please assist us by concentrating on what you're being asked, which is: What did you personally see from the observation post at 4.00 in the morning roughly. I know you didn't have a watch and you're not is sure of the time, but just let's proceed on that basis, what you actually saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At 4.00 in the morning, we heard the noise of the vehicles, and this entered -- this noise entered Stagova at Rruga e Kuqe and Dardha. We did not see them, but we heard the noises. But then, an hour later, the police forces and the army forces entered -- came close to Mahalla e Gudaqeve. We were closer there, so we saw them from the observation point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Let me back you up a minute. Did you ever leave the first observation point?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First observation point, yes, I left. I went close to the soldiers. I don't know why I went, to get a glass of water or to light a cigarette, but it was for only about ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And from that second location, could you see army forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a flat area there, and from there you can see the forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Scully, I would much prefer if you would ask him what he saw rather than questions like: Could you see army forces? That is a leading question and the answer to that is not going to be of any assistance to us from a witness like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: All right. We're kind of having to go the long way around to get there, but I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understood there was some exercise called proofing undertaken with witnesses before they came into court. Has that happened with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Where did you go after you left -- I'm sorry, where did you go after you had the glass of water and saw the persons on the flat part?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I had to go to my family -- not my immediate family, but my nephews and nieces were there. And I told Shabedin to go to his house because he had his people there. I told Muhamet to go to his house as well, to tell those people what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What happened after you did that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I woke them up, and there was somebody who accompanied these people to a hiding place, to a kind of shelter. So the evacuation process happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, this is a very big case which involves many allegations, all of which have to be explored within a reasonable time by this Court. We don't have time to hear all about the drinks of water, the cigarettes, the visits to relatives, and so on that you feel the need to tell us about. We need to know about the activities of people who are engaged in conflict or doing things that they shouldn't be doing, either in a conflict or non-conflict situation. We are not here to learn all about life in your particular village at that time. Now, do you understand that? Now, when you're being asked questions, you should concentrate on what you're being asked. We're getting a completely different story today from you about the weapons, for example, that were available to you as a KLA unit from the story you gave us the other day, and we're concerned about that. We are very anxious that we're not getting a full account from you of what really matters in this case. So please concentrate on the issues. Listen carefully to Mr. Scully's questions, and if the difficulty continues I will take over the questioning. Now, do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, clarification on the record. He described the KLA units in the village with some heavy weaponry. Today he's described that he was not a part of that unit but was instead part of a separate group of civilians who were at an observation post. That separate group of civilians was armed with an M-48 rifle. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just give me a moment here. I have a 65 ter summary in this case which says that in the last months of the conflict he served as a member of a local KLA unit. There were 15 members in the unit, and in the early May 1999 they started a 24-month -- sorry, 24-hour watch for Serbian troops. Now, is this a different unit from the one that we were told about on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: There are two units in a previous statement he --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, just answer yes or no. You're saying it's a different unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: That is a different unit from the unit at the observation post. The confusion arises --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And should I be clear about that from the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I can direct you to the exact parts of the transcript from Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: The confusion may arise because the civilian unit in the statement and probably in the 65 ter summary has been described as a civilian component to the larger KLA unit, but what he's testified to today and what's borne out by the statements and the 65 ter summary is that it was a separate group of people, no matter what you call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Tell me where in the transcript I find this.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Looking at -- it's 45, 23, starting at about page -- page 2. So it says, so a unit was formed, they were kind of defending the population from this oppression, and then from that line on it describes how the unit was armed. And then I asked him today: Were you part of that unit? And the answer was: No, he was part of a separate group of civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me -- so this didn't emerge on Monday. You're saying it emerged today?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. No. He has always said that he was a part of a separate group of people --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, tell me where that is in the transcript from the 9th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: No, the 9th of October we were not talking about his role in the unit. We were talking about his knowledge that it existed and what it did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. So it's today that I should have realised there were two units?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: That -- well, yes. And the confusion is that we thought it was sort of two parts of the same unit, and what he's telling us today is that it was in fact completely separate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let me get that in today's transcript. Where do I find that today? You see, your question was at the beginning today: "Directing your attention to the unit that spontaneously formed in the village, did you have any role with that? "No, absolutely not."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I apologise. And he then says: "I had this" -- "No, absolutely not. I had this observation point. We only observed from that point. "And then who was observing from the observation point?" And then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you're surprised that I think that was a change of position from Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: No -- I guess. I'm hoping it's clear now. He also says, you know, who were these people at the observation point? We were all civilians. Whereas the unit we described on Monday were not civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, where do I see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: It's line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On page?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: "We were all civilians, yes." But I assumed that that was him talking about this spontaneously formed unit, which is the starting point for your questions. I don't see a distinction here between two units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he said he was not part of the spontaneously formed unit; that's the: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Very well. Well, let's carry on and see what we can actually hear that he experienced on the 21st of May, because at the moment there's nothing of value in this evidence and we've now had half an hour of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, could you see what happened in the village of Stagovo on the 21st of May?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could see what was happening, not only me but others as well. On the 21st of May, a little bit after 9.00, I went to the place where the KLA was because there was no other place for us to go. And from there we could observe what was going on in the whole terrain. We could see everything, even the forces moving along the railroad, the Serbian police was patrolling there, they were firing from their weapons, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What were they shooting at?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I might have not mentioned it before, but I have brought a tape here. To your question what they were shooting at, they were shooting at everything they could, civilians, everything they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did you ever see anything lit on fire that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What was lit on fire?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At approximately 10.00, houses began to burn.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: About how many houses did you see begin to burn?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many houses. We couldn't count them right away, but later on we counted that 96 out of 182 were burned, completely. Some other houses were burned, but not destroyed completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: While you were watching that day, did you ever see any civilians try to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see civilians try to leave the village. It is important to mention the position of Stagova. People were not -- it was not possible for them to leave because Stagova is on a valley. We could see people moving in the direction of Nerodime but they stopped there. They could not leave because of the river.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What time did the shooting stop?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting stopped at 1700 hours, and they began to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did you ever go down to the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What did you find when you got there?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Horror. We found victims killed in the most barbarian way. Then we started to gather the civilians and to put them in the remaining houses that were not damaged for shelter. It was also dangerous because of the fact that the area around the place where the massacre was committed was mined. We didn't know that, but luckily some animals had entered that area and the mines were set out -- set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: How many persons killed did you personally see?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw all the persons that were dead, that were killed. We didn't touch them for security reasons, but we could see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Can you tell me the number of persons killed that you saw?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There I saw 10 persons who had been killed that day, on the 21st of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did you know the names of any of those 10?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I know them. Some of them were guests, people who were visiting in Stagova, while others were villagers from Stagova itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Can you tell us the names and approximate ages of the people you did know?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I will start with Fitim Gudaqi, 7 year old; Ramadan Dashi; Brahim Dashi; Hamdi Dashi; then the grandmother of Fitim Gudaqi. I can't remember her name at the moment. She was more than 80 years old. She couldn't even walk. She was carried in a horse-drawn cart. Then the wife of -- I don't remember his wife, but you can see it on the tape. Then it was Bela and Rrushi; these were people who were visiting in Stagova at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Do you remember any other names of the people you saw killed on May 21st?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the moment, I can't remember exactly. But they are on the tape and I can tell them by names, but at the moment I cannot recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Were any of the people you saw killed there wearing a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them were civilians. All of the victims were civilians. None of them was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did any of them have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: You've spoken about some houses you saw burnt. Could you tell if they were burnt from the inside or the outside?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the houses were burnt from the inside. There were houses that were hit from the outside as well. The school building, Agim Bajrami's school building also was damaged and the mosque as well. The school was burned from the inside, and the library, the school library as well. As for the mosque, you can still see traces of shells on the walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Do you know if other bodies besides the ones you've described personally seeing were found in Kacanik -- I'm sorry, were found in Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 21st of May that year, we saw these bodies that I mentioned. And two other bodies were a little bit further up. The body of Ramush Jaha and Fahri Mani, they were also killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Do you know those person's ages?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fahri was more or less 60 years old, while the other one was quite older. He was the oldest man in Stagova, between 80 and 90 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: During the entire day of the 21st of May, did you ever fire a weapon?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not only me, but those others who were there, they didn't fire a weapon as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: What is the ethnic balance of the municipality of Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only Albanians in Stagova, no other ethnic groups. At least to my recollection there have not been other ethnic groups in Stagova proper. However, in Stagova municipality there were other ethnic groups. There were Serbs in Kacanik i Vjeter, in the town of Kacanik, and the majority of them lived and still lives in Shterpca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scully, just one moment. Do you wish to try to assist us further in relation to the beginning of the event, now that you've got obviously the witness attuned to the idea of what he should be trying to concentrate on?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a matter for you, but if you think -- I mean, I think the whole -- the start of this event is very confusing. If you don't think it can be clarified, then fine; but if you think it can, then you should try.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I don't think it's going to get much clearer in terms of who arrived when.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: If the Court has questions on where he was and what he was able to observe, we could go further into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I was more concerned about whether he could identify who was arriving and from where they came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I don't think we're going to get much better on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks very much. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we will proceed in the following manner: General Pavkovic, General Lukic, General Lazarevic, Mr. Milutinovic, Mr. Sainovic, and General Ojdanic. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, I expect to be very brief with you. I'm interested in this KLA group of 15 persons that you may or may not have been a member of. When you from your observation post heard that people were advancing towards Stagovo, where were these 15 armed KLA members at that time? They were down in the village, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And when they learned that these forces were advancing, they started shooting at them, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: During that time I was there, and they didn't fire at all, absolutely not. They sheltered at Kulla e Cakes. There was no other place for them to shelter. It was impossible to shoot at a force of that size.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, these forces that were approaching, did they see -- did they see these 15 KLA men leave the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How did they manage to get out of the village without being seen by these forces that were approaching?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA unit did not leave the village. They existed in the peripheral parts of the village, in the outskirts, in Mahalla e Gudaqeve and at the neighbourhood of Dashi. They moved around. They existed in Stagova as well, but then there is a mountain near the railroad and you cannot go any further. This is where they were stationed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we started this examination with my question of asking you if they were in the village as these forces were approaching; you told me they were. Now, having told me they were there, there must have been a time when they left the village. And my question was now: Did they leave a village in such a way that these advancing forces could have seen them leave? And I think your answer is: No. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, I will repeat it again. The place where the KLA was staying was not detected, could not be seen. They moved along the outskirts of Stagova up to the Kulla e Cakes and they stayed there. They did not operate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, there was a time when you left the operation post that you were at. Let me just back up a minute. Tell us, in relation to the centre of your village, where was this observation post that you were observing from? How far away from your village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The houses in Stagova are scattered. It is divided into two neighbourhoods, neighbourhood number one and number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm interested in where you were. Where were you observing from, how far from the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I live in neighbourhood two. My house is there. And we were observing in the direction of Stagova fields, in the direction of the main road in case they entered our village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So you were actually in the village when you were observing?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the outskirts of the village. You could only see one part of the village; you could not see the whole village of Stagova from that observation post. It is high ground. It is a mountainous area; therefore, you could not see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, there came a time when you left that observation post and joined up with the other 15 KLA from your village, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, I don't remember exactly. I went to the second place --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now, where was it that you joined up with these other 15 KLA men from your village? From your observation post, where did you go to join up with them?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question; it's not clear to me. When I left the first time, as I said I went to have a glass of water or smoke a cigarette, and the second time I went to inform my extended family about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: If the question wasn't clear to you, why did you try to answer it? I will make the clear now. You joined up with these other 15 KLA men from your village. My question is: Where did you join up with them? Where?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kulla e Cakes, where they were stationed. After I went to my house, I went to Kulla e Cakes and joined the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was about a hundred metres from where you had been observing, wasn't it, very close?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The post from where I was observing was not further than 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Isn't that what I just said, that you went with these 15 men to a place a hundred metres from where you had been observing. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Objection. Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Scully -- Mr. Ackerman, I'm happy with the -- that the answer is a hundred metres -- less than a hundred metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I am, too, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement which you gave to the Prosecution on 6 June of 1999, it reflects that you said this: "I went and joined up with the other 15 KLA men from my village," leaving the implication at least that you were part of the KLA from your village and you just joined up with the other 15 members of the KLA. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I were a KLA member, I would have told you that. I wasn't. And not only me, the other civilians as well were with them. We were kind of support to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, that's very confusing, sir, because in your statement to the OTP back in 1999, what you told them then was: "I had never been a member of the UCK until about two months ago. There were very few weapons available for Albanians and I became mobilised." So you did become a member of the KLA, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't a member of the KLA. I'm emphasising again: If I were a KLA member I wouldn't keep it a secret. It would be an honour for me to tell you that. But as I said, there was a lack of weapons as well, and it wasn't possible for people to join.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, when you spoke of -- you know, I don't understand why you said in your statement to the OTP that you'd never been a member until two months ago when you were mobilised if you weren't ever a member. I mean, how does that make sense?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat it again. I was not a KLA soldier. If that is what the statement says, then it's a mistake. I was not a KLA soldier; if I was, it would have been an honour. We only dealt with civilian issues. Due to the lack of weapons, the KLA did not function in Stagova. I could not get a weapon, otherwise I would have joined the KLA, not in Stagova but I would have joined the 162nd Brigade. Therefore, as I already told you, we only looked after civilians and observed the terrain. I joined up with the KLA on the day of the offensive, on the 21st of May. I joined up with the unit in Stagova on this date.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. What you then said in your statement after you said you had joined up with them a hundred metres from where you had been observing, you then said: "We were armed with machine-guns and Kalashnikovs and one mortar gun. That was all we had." So you were armed at that point apparently with a Kalashnikov at least, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you say that: "We decided not to fire at the Serbs advancing from the west." At this point where you got together up there on the hill. "We did not want to put the civilians at further risk." Now, can I conclude from that that you -- that they had been firing at the Serbs advancing prior to that point? Isn't that a fair conclusion from that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can say whatever you want, but not a single shot was fired in the direction of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, from this position up there where you were with the -- the KLA unit, armed with machine-guns and Kalashnikovs and mortars -- and a mortar gun, you couldn't actually see anyone get killed in your village, could you?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We learned about the massacre that had been committed at 10.00 in the morning. Xhevat Mani with two of his in-laws came and told me what had happened. The majority of the civilians were caught and put in the house of Enver Jaha. We could not act in any way. Maybe we would have acted if it was possible, but the civilians were captured and we couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The answer is: No, you didn't see anyone get killed. Isn't that the answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see them getting killed because the place where the massacre was committed could not be seen from where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And as far as you know, 10 persons were killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14 were killed, 12 were injured. These were the figures of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you call this a massacre?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Objection. Argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, if the question relates to language used by the witness, then it can hardly be described as argumentative. Carry on, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You call this a massacre?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen a more savage killing than this. How can you not call it a massacre when a 7-year-old child was killed and a 80, 90-year-old man? You can see the tape and you can see for yourself that it was a massacre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: How many people were left alive in the village after this incident?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, this question is taking me back. From the 1st of May, many villagers left the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I want to know when you went back to the village after this event how many people were left alive in the village, how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now are into a debate of argument, Mr. Ackerman. Obviously everyone but 14. Unless your question relates to whether there had been movement away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm just wondering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you want to clarify it that way and make it clear it's not argumentative, then fine. But if this is simply a debate about whether 14 deaths amount to a massacre, then this isn't the place for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's not, Your Honour. I want to know how many people were there when he went back into the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you answer that, please, Mr. Dashi, how many people were in the village after the event was over?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't tell you exactly how many remained, but there were about a hundred people who were not captured by the Serbian forces. The Serbian forces caught these 50 people, and of these 50 people, 14 were killed and about 12 were injured. Some of them were from Biceci. There were some nieces there. They remained alive in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You gave an additional statement to the Prosecutor on 10 March 2002, where you were talking about identification of -- of these forces. And what you said in the one, two, three, four, fifth paragraph is: "The truth is we were provided with a description of the uniforms by other people. I saw the Serb forces myself. However, I was unable to discern their uniforms." That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only at that time, but even today it's difficult for me to discern, to identify them, because I'm not good at colours at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You left your village on 27 May of 1999, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And no one forced you to leave, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, in answer to one of Mr. Ackerman's questions you said that you were armed with a Kalashnikov.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you were initially at 4.00 in the morning in the observation post, were you armed then with a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How then did you come by the weapon in the course of the day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the soldiers of the KLA -- one of the soldiers was ill and he gave me his weapon. He was very ill. It was his weapon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Now Mr. Lukic -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, I'm advised that these statements I referred to are actually in e-court as 5D8 and 5D9, and since I referred to them I'll now tender them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi, my name is Branko Lukic. I have a couple of questions for you. Although it was very difficult to capture all the discrepancies between your various statements and testimony, may we now clarify certain points. Were you mobilised by the KLA or were you not mobilised by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not armed and I was not a soldier. I got the rifle on the 21st of May, 1999, at Kulla e Cakes. One soldier was ill, I got his weapon. I was not mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So if in your statement given to the OTP says that you were mobilised by the KLA, that is not correct, right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat it. I was not a soldier. If I had been, I would have been proud of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's not correct; that's all I'm interested in. If something like that is written, that is not correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, we've been over this with Mr. Ackerman. The position is clear. All the witness is doing is repeating for I think for the fourth time, the same answer. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the commander of the unit that you joined as you say on the 21st of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remzi Krraba.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also knew of the existence of the 162nd Brigade. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you knew that that brigade counted about a thousand men?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That brigade was active in the area of your village and the surrounding villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It operated in the Sharri mountains, not in my village, absolutely not. It did not operate there, because there is the main road, Pristina-Skup [as interpreted], that divides my village from the Sharri mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Around that road are located the following villages in which the 162nd Brigade was active. I will now read out to you the names of these villages and you will confirm to me that the 162nd Brigade existed in those villages: Raka, Grlica, Doganovic, Stari Kacanik, Duskaja, Dubrava, Runjevo, Kovacevac, Gajre, Ivaja, Djurdjevdo. All these villages are in the immediate vicinity of yours. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Stagova borders these villages. Stagova, in fact, borders Biqeznik [phoen] and a couple of other villages, but the other ones that you mentioned are not close to Stagova. They are on the other side of the main road. From Stagova to Biqez it's about 5 to 6 kilometres, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's precisely what I am asserting.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One more thing, if I'm allowed, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you haven't answered the question as yet, so please try to do that. The question was whether the KLA were -- the 162nd Brigade were active in these villages, to your knowledge. Now, what's the answer to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It could be said so, but the reality is that the 162nd Brigade operated in the Sharri mountains. But in order to get food supplies and other supplies that the army needed, they might have gone to the -- to these villages. Otherwise, they did not enter these villages; they stayed away from these villages. This is what I heard. There was no KLA in Grlice because the police forces were there. In Kacanik as well, because the police station was there, in Stari Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that you were at a scouting post. Who told you to go there, to this reconnaissance or scouting post?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody sent me there. We had to do it because we had to observe the terrain, because at any moment we were expecting the forces to come. They came to other villages as well, not only to my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So is it the case that there were two groups in your village, one numbering 15 armed men belonging to the KLA, and another group scouting from that observation post? Is that what you are saying today?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that the men from the KLA knew that you were at that observation or scouting post?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They might have known or they might not have known. We, as citizens, we did the observation ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that those members of the KLA were in your village. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Today on page 12, line 3, when responding to a question from my learned friend from the Prosecution, who asked you if you had seen what was going on in the village, you answered: "We were able to see what was going on." In contrast, on page 3, line 10, also today, you say: "We did not see the village, just the road from Urosevac to Kacanik." If you did not see the village, just the road, how were you able to see what was going on in the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Objection. That mischaracterises. He was describing two different locations in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not at the moment until we resolve this, please. Well, Mr. Lukic, it's a matter for you how you go about this, but I've no recollection of the witness saying -- giving any evidence about observing anything within -- occurring within the built-up part of the village. And, really, it's that that matters, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I noted something like that on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if it would be helpful, page 22, line 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Also this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "We didn't see them getting killed because the place where the massacre was committed could not been seen from where we were."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. But the point I'm making, as I have no -- unless Mr. Lukic has a different recollection, I don't think that the witness has claimed to have seen anything actually happening within the village, and therefore we're on an academic point it would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 12, line 3 the question was: "Mr. Dashi" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've got that, Mr. Lukic. But what does he say he actually saw happening? I'm making the point to you. Did he actually give any concrete evidence about seeing something happen in the village himself? And if he didn't, are we not really debating an academic point?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, maybe Mr. Scully has a different point of view. Did he claim to see anything in the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: He describes forces shooting at everything and houses burning, although he was also clear that he could not see anyone actually get killed. I wasn't sure where the question was going --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But this is on page 12 again, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Page 12, line 12, Your Honour. To your question: "What were they shooting at? "They were shooting at everything they could, at civilians."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But all the -- the only evidence he's given is of seeing forces moving along the railroad. I'm sorry? Yeah, but he doesn't say what he saw happening. I mean, it's pointless to have evidence: I could see everything that was happening and then he doesn't say what he actually saw. We don't have any evidence as a result of that. That's the only point I'm trying to make. But if you think that's important, please carry on and cross-examine on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll have to clarify some more points on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi, is it true that on that day in your village there were 3.000 people?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never said that, that on the 21st of March -- of May there were 3.000 people in my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said your village had a population of 1600 and that together with the people who had come from other places, there were 3.000.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population was 1.600, a little more maybe. I spoke in approximate terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what may we conclude then, that on that day in your village there were 1600 people?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How many people were there on that day in your village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Stagova was overcrowded because during the past two weeks people were coming from other villages and going towards Skopije by train. Other people remained there, but on the 21st of May, the train did not stop at Stagova. So the people who were there, the civilians, went to the Jaha stream and they remained there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the number? How many people were there in your village on the 21st of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could have been 150, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So all the people had already left the village before any of the fighting began?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in Stagova, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, this is important, Mr. Dashi. I mean, what had happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not clear about the people who remained in Stagova or what are you asking me about? Could you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If there had been 3.000 people there and there were only 150 on the 21st of May and 10 per cent of them were KLA terrorists, it's quite an important fact in connection with the activity of the Serb forces that day. So I would like to be clear, if you can assist me, in establishing exactly how many people were there first thing in the morning of the 21st of May. Was it only 150 people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The train did not stop there that day. It didn't even come that way. So the people who went to the stream and remained there because of the police forces, some of them went to Begrac from Mahalla e Hysajre to Begrac. They wanted to go there, they could go there. The rest remained in Stagova.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So at 4.00 in the morning when you observed or heard activity of vehicles, how many people were actually resident in Stagova?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 150. I don't think there were more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where were the other 2.850?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The influx of refugees happened two weeks ago. They want -- they came to Stagova because there was a train station there, and from there you could go to Skopije. So that's what we did. We helped these people, we sheltered them in the houses, and then they took the train and went to Skopije.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Let's leave them aside. 1600 inhabitants of Stagova itself, the people who were normally resident there, where were the other 1.450 of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They went to other places. They went to Skopije by train.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So this was like a ghost village on the day that this happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. My family, for example, left on the 1st of May and went to Skopije.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I have to say, Mr. Scully, I had no impression of this village being like that on this day. Should I have had that impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is unfortunately news to me too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just -- I should also say at this stage that it may be that my impression of how much the witness has claimed to be able to see in the village is not that held by everyone. So if you do wish to cross-examine further on that, then that may be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi, when exactly did you learn that there were no longer any people in that village, already at 4.00 a.m. on the 21st of May, 1999, in the village there were no more than 150 people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned this because from my neighbourhood there were people, but from neighbourhood number one there were no people there. I learned it earlier that there was this influx of people and people moving and going towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did your wife leave for Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of May of the same year.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your entire family left with her. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The civilians who were surrounded were surrounded by the paramilitaries. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitaries were seen. I did not see them myself, but paramilitaries and police forces were seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should I take you back to your statement or will you take my word for it that in your statement you said they had been surrounded by the paramilitaries? Do you remember stating that to the Office of the Prosecutor earlier and that that was the reason why you did not fire at the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question? It's not clear to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could have the exact reference from the statement, I think those answers will reconcile themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, is the -- is it the statement 5D8 or 5D9?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Statement 5D8 -- give me one second. Yes, now I finally -- it's -- give me one second. In English version it's page number 3, paragraph number 2; Albanian version, page number 3, paragraph number 3; and Serbian version, page number 3, paragraph number 2. And it says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you want it on e-court?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If possible, yes, please, in Albanian for this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's have the Albanian page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Paragraph number 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's 5D8.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I have an Albanian language hard copy as well, if that would assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would help, but I think we're almost there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Page number 3, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Dashi, if you look at page 3 of your statement, at paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Second sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here: "We were going to fight back and fire at the Serbs, but we were warned by a civilian from the village that the civilian population had been trying to flee towards the north, but they were surrounded by paramilitaries. When we heard this, we decided not to fire at the Serbs advancing from the west." This passage in your statement given to the Prosecutor, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So your testimony on the record today is not correct that they were surrounded by the paramilitaries and the police?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true. What I said today is true. A mistake has occurred with the statement. It is true that the civilians were surrounded and that we were unable to act because of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the same paragraph, in the following sentence, you say: "From my position I could not see where the civilian population was." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the position where we were, civilians leaving Prroni i Jahes were seen and -- at 10.00 a.m., and they walked towards the fields in the direction of Nerodime and that's where they remained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In other words, this part of the statement that you provided to the Prosecutor of this Tribunal is also not correct. Are you saying now that you actually saw where the civilians were? Did you personally see where the civilians were?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't answer that for a moment. Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's the same problem as earlier. The witness talks about stuff he observed from two different locations. If you go down in the statement, he then talks about a group of 10 to 15 women and children he saw leaving the village. In the section that counsel was originally referring to, he says he could not see where the civilian population where when they were surrounded by paramilitaries. So if counsel can pick which paragraph he is referring to, the answer might be clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think that I couldn't be more precise. I was referring to paragraph number 3 from the page number 3, Albanian version, and it's the second sentence after the one we were discussing before. So I was asking him about the situation when civilians were surrounded by some forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, how do we know that the answer given at line 19 on page 35 is not a reference to the later part of what's in his statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can try to clarify that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll clarify it when we come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will need to break now and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00. Mr. Dashi, we'll have to have a break for 20 minutes. You'll be shown again where to wait, and we'll see you again at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Lukic will continue, Mr. Dashi. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, we have to clarify a certain matter, as instructed by the Trial Chamber. You were in two places on the 21st of May, 1999. From which of these places could you see the Urosevac-Kacanik road?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the observation post, while when I joined up with the army at Kulla e Cakes, from there you can no longer see the main road. From there you can see Stagova.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which part of Stagovo could you observe from that other place?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the second place, that is neighbourhood number two, which is at the north-east of Stagova, you can see the place where the massacre was committed but you cannot see the area around the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you now saying that you did see with your own two eyes the massacre, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not see with my own eyes the massacre. That area is a mountainous area, and there is a stream, a brook. You can see the neighbourhood and Prroni i Jahes, but they were deeper in that area and we could not see the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us that the vehicles of the Serb forces stopped some 300 metres away from the village. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not more than that. At Rruga e Kuqe, or the red road, where I was observing, it is not more than 300 metres, while the road that takes you to the martyrs' cemetery is a little further up, and both these roads joined the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How long did it take them to do the 300 metres?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important to emphasise that it was early in the morning and we could hear the noise. So when they came down to Mahalle e Gudaqeve, that's where I could see and hear the noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How much time passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 20 minutes. I will -- I would ask you to repeat it again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe that we received an answer. Are you saying that 20 minutes passed from the moment the troops left their vehicles to the moment when they entered the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: So at Mahalle e Gudaqeve, which is close, it was only 20 minutes. And as for the other parts, it must have been later on. I couldn't have seen them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're saying that the troops were shooting all that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the period of time later, yes; but if you're referring at the moment when they came to Mahalle e Gudaqeve, part of them remained at the mountain and they were shooting from there, while another part was walking in the direction of Mahalle e Gudaqeve.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But the shooting went on all this time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to 5.00, plus/minus 15 minutes. It didn't stop at all up to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who were the troops shooting at, bearing in mind that the troops were both in the village and outside the village?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure as far as the troops outside are concerned. However, the troops that were inside, which we were observing, they were shooting wherever they could. They were shooting at the houses, they were shooting at the animals. They killed all the animals that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: According to you, the troops that from very early morning until 5.00 in the afternoon kept on opening fire killed a total of 12 people or 14 people?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were there any KLA units in the territory of your village?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that's been asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've told us that on the uniforms worn by some of the troops you saw the inscription "police," "milicija." From what distance could you see that word, "milicija"?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very true that Kulla e Cakes is on high ground. Along the railroad they approached our position. I would say that they were at 60 metres from us, and we could see them with binoculars.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On which sleeve and in which letter was this inscription?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inscription "milicija" in their language -- was in their language, and I think it was on the left upper arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, the evidence will show that this is practically impossible, that you could not have seen that in 1999. How do you explain the fact that you did not see any insignia on the uniform, but at the same time you observed the word "milicija" in the Cyrillic script?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true that I did not see the uniform. I only said that I'm not good in colours to treat this matter accurately. I have seen the uniform; I saw it very well, but I'm not able to describe it. I might make mistakes. I'm here to tell you the truth, and I stand by what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Dashi. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. We don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No questions for this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to have one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi, at one point you told us you took a Kalashnikov and joined the 14 members of the KLA. Am I right? You took the Kalashnikov from the 15th member who was ill at the time. This is what you stated today. Is it true?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's true. In other words, it was given to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's move on quickly, please. You said you were not a member of the KLA. I can assume then that on that day you wore civilian clothes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: At the moment when you were holding the Kalashnikov and when you saw the group of 15 KLA members, you were still wearing civilian clothes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The other members of the KLA, did they wear uniforms or did they wear civilian clothes? This is my question.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some who were wearing uniforms and some who were wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dashi, just a few questions for you. Can you please tell me whether you know that on the 27th of March there was a fighting -- and I am referring to the year 1999, that there was fighting between the KLA and the Serb forces in the town of Kacanik in the part known as Ladjatere [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Laxha e Re [phoen], if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Are you familiar with the fact that there was fighting there?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Dashi, the village of Runjevo is between Kacanik and Stagovo. Am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Runjeva is between Kacanik and Stagova. It's situated on the railroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And the distance between Kacanik and Stagovo is some 5 or 6 kilometres. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Dashi, in the month of March, on the 27th of March and a few days afterwards, did a number of people from Kacanik arrive in your village? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is very true. There was a great influx of people who came to Stagova. Some of them sheltered in the village, some sheltered in the mountains, some went to Krivanjev [phoen] --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm going to ask you about that. Mr. Dashi, was your village of Stagovo ever under the control of the KLA from the beginning of war that started on the 24th of March, 1999, onwards?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it never was. If you want me to explain, to my knowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is enough. I'll ask you a few more questions about that.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- the KLA operated in Sharri mountains.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Were there any KLA members in Runjevo, which is also on the railway -- road?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that at the beginning of April there was an April in Runjevo between the Serb forces and the KLA and that on that occasion some 50 KLA members were either killed or hurt? Are you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in Laxha e Re in Kacanik, not in Runjeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the beginning of April and not about the 27th of March. I'm asking you about the beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well then. In your village, was there any other KLA unit in addition to the unit that you've been mentioning?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no other unit except for the one that I mentioned in the village of Stagova. I would like to add something here. There were young men from Stagova who were KLA members, but they were not in Stagova, they were operating in other areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the basis for my question was Exhibit 3D100, page 11, and I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic. Mr. Scully.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, when you were together -- when you were with the 15 KLA members, did that group stay together for the entire day?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So at around 8.00 I joined up with this group, and I didn't leave this group until 5.00. So we spent the whole night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: And were you ever directly shot at by any of the forces you've described that day?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were shootings directed at us, but this place where we were was on high ground and luckily they didn't hit us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Scully, 8.00 and 5.00, is that a period of 21 hours or are we talking about just overnight? Could --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think this needs to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Mr. Dashi, do you mean 5.00 in the morning or 5.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1700 hours. I apologise. So from 8.00 in the morning till 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So the next part of the answer then doesn't make sense: "So we spent the whole night there."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Unless it's a translation problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I don't know if it is or not. I can -- I'll just ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: Did -- where did you spend the previous night to the 21st, the night of the 20th?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Stagova. If you have patience, I will explain it to you. On the 21st of May from 8.00 I joined up with the KLA unit, and I stayed with them till 1700 hours. We observed the terrain. We saw the victims, and we spent the night with them. There was no other place that we could go.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCULLY
utterances.text: How many neighbourhoods are there in the municipality of -- or in the village of Stagovo?

utterances.speaker: MUHARREM DASHI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are two neighbourhoods. As for mahallas, you have the Jahaj mahalla, the Manaj mahalla, the Brahaj mahalla, the mahalla of Gudaqeve, the mahalla of Bajrami, the mahalla of Hysi.
